newsitem.title: USA: NW Ohio SRW wheat looks better than last year-tour.
newsitem.headline: NW Ohio SRW wheat looks better than last year-tour.

text.p: Soft red winter wheat yield potential in northwest Ohio looked well above last year and mostly above average, participants on one of seven routes on the first day of the annual SRW wheat crop tour said.

After surveying six fields in six counties, participants calculated an average potential yield of 66 bushels per acre in a range of 54 to 82 bushels, well ahead of last year's actual yields for the same group of counties and slightly ahead of two years ago.
The group surveyed fields in Lucas, Fulton, Williams, Defiance, Paulding and Van Wert counties.
Participants said they detected some evidence of powdery mildew in one field in Lucas County where the wheat was just beginning to head.
"I'm expecting the wheat to outgrow the powdery mildew as the temperatures warm up in northwestern Ohio," said tour leader Jim Quinton of Consolidated Grain and Barge Co.
The forecast for northwestern Ohio for Monday was for warm and windy conditions with a high of 75 degrees Fahrenheit.
In 1996, yields for those six counties ranged from 44.1 to 56.1 bushels per acre, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
"That was a disease-ridden year where the crop was hurt by head scab and chronic disease," Quinton said.
Head scab is a fungal disease that attacks the wheat heads in the developing kernel.
Participants on another route in southeast Michigan, contacted by telephone after touring seven fields in two counties, said they found the wheat to be almost disease-free.
"We have done Monroe County, the furthest east and south county in Michigan, and Lenawee County," said Marvin Hodgson, a grain merchandiser with The Andersons Inc.
"In Monroe County, we had some wheat that is flowering. There was very, very little disease. We saw the lightest disease pressure we have ever seen in five years."
That group saw yields ranging from 56 to 82 bushels per acre for the two counties.
"We have been in some fields that have the potential for 100 bushels per acre," Hodgson said. "That is exceptional. The wheat is fully headed."

About 21 participants including grain merchandisers, agronomists and USDA officials, were on the first leg of the tour which will cover roughly 15 counties in northwest Ohio, five counties in northeast Indiana and three counties in southeast Michigan.
Another 40 participants were expected to join the tour on the second and third days. On Tuesday, participants will scout areas in southern Illinois, southwest Indiana and western Kentucky.
The tour, sponsored by the Wheat Quality Council, will conclude on Wednesday in Little Rock, Arkansas, after participants examine fields in the bootheel area of Missouri and in eastern Arkansas.
